prompt: What makes a restore drill different from the restores in lessons 1 to 6?
hint: The value is in doing it again.

choices.text: It restores over the live database to test it for real
choices.why: A drill never touches the live database; it restores somewhere harmless.

choices.text: It uses a logical dump instead of a physical backup
choices.why: It uses whatever the real recovery would use, here pgBackRest.

choices.text: Repetition: scheduled, timed, recorded
choices.why: Right. A failure shows up in the week it happens, and the timings show a trend.

choices.text: It skips the comparison to save time on large databases
choices.why: The comparison is the proof; skipping it turns a drill back into a claim.

prompt: Which question can only a drill answer, among the checks in this course?
hint: Lesson 8 needs a number.

choices.text: How long a restore of the real data takes
choices.why: Right. Only a timed restore of the real data measures it.

choices.text: Whether the archive command succeeded last night
choices.why: pg_stat_archiver and check answer that.

choices.text: Whether the repository files match their checksums
choices.why: verify answers that.

choices.text: Whether the nightly job exited with 0
choices.why: The job's own exit status says that.

prompt: Why does the platform's drill restore to a new, temporary server rather than over the database it tests?
hint: Which operation is the destructive one?

choices.text: Because the cloud provider forbids restoring over a live instance
choices.why: The reason is about risk, not a provider's rule.

choices.text: To save money on storage
choices.why: A second server costs more, not less.

choices.text: Because the live database would be faster afterwards
choices.why: Speed is not involved.

choices.text: A restore over it destroys what you need if the restore is bad
choices.why: Right. The restore is the destructive act, and it would destroy the thing being tested.

prompt: What does `\gexec` do at the end of the first query in `report.sql`?
hint: The query returns statements.

choices.text: Exports the result to a file
choices.why: Writing to a file is \o or \copy; \gexec executes.

choices.text: Runs each returned row as SQL
choices.why: Right: it runs each row the query returned as a statement. The query writes one statement per table.

choices.text: Repeats the query every few seconds
choices.why: That is \watch.

choices.text: Runs the query inside a single transaction
choices.why: \gexec does not open a transaction.

prompt: Why does `report.sql` read `information_schema.tables` instead of naming the shop's tables?
hint: What happens the day somebody adds a table?

choices.text: Naming tables is not allowed in a report
choices.why: It is allowed; lesson 1's verify.sql did it.

choices.text: New tables join the drill unedited
choices.why: Right. A report that names tables silently stops covering the database as it grows.

choices.text: information_schema is faster to read than the tables
choices.why: It is a catalogue view; speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Tables named directly might be locked during a drill
choices.why: Naming them changes nothing about locking.

prompt: One row of three million has one character changed in the restored copy, and the total is unchanged. Which report notices?
hint: Lesson 1's sums against this lesson's fingerprints.

choices.text: Both: any change moves a sum
choices.why: A changed name does not move a sum of totals, and two changes can cancel.

choices.text: Neither: one row in three million is below what a report can detect
choices.why: The fingerprint detects one character anywhere in any row.

choices.text: Lesson 1's report only, because it sums columns
choices.why: A sum over total_cents cannot see a change in another column.

choices.text: This lesson's fingerprint, and not lesson 1's sums
choices.why: Right. md5 over every row's text changes with one character; a sum over one column does not see a changed name.

prompt: About how many seconds did `report.sql` take on `bigshop`?
hint: The real line of time.

prompt: Put the drill script's steps in order.
hint: The moment has to exist before anything is restored to it.
items: Create a restore point and read the live reports
Wait until the archive has the restore point
Restore to the second server and start it
Read the reports on the copy and compare
Throw the copy away and append a line to drills.csv
trap: The target is named first; check makes sure it is archived; restore and recovery come next; the proof needs the copy; and the copy goes, with a record, whatever the result.

prompt: In the first drill, which phase took longest, and why?
hint: Restore 2.2 s, recovery 2.5 s, proof 6.0 s.

choices.text: The proof, because it reads every row on both sides
choices.why: Right. Fingerprinting three million rows means reading and sorting them.

choices.text: The restore, because it decompresses every file
choices.why: It took 2.2 seconds, the shortest phase.

choices.text: The recovery, because it replays the archive
choices.why: 2.5 seconds; there was little log to replay.

choices.text: They were equal
choices.why: 6.0 is more than twice either of the others.

prompt: Why does the script remove the restored copy whatever the result?
hint: What is left running otherwise, and with what in it?

choices.text: Because pgBackRest refuses to restore twice into the same directory
choices.why: It could restore with --delta; that is not the reason.

choices.text: Because a restored copy slows down the live server
choices.why: It shares the machine here, and that is not why it is removed.

choices.text: So a failed drill does not leave a server holding the data
choices.why: Right. A drill that fails is exactly when a forgotten copy is left behind.

choices.text: So that the next backup is smaller
choices.why: Backups come from the live server; the copy has nothing to do with them.

prompt: How many seconds did the first drill take in total?
hint: The sixth field.

prompt: The second drill reported `DIFFERENT` although the backup was perfect. What caused it?
hint: Compare when each side was read.

choices.text: The restore point was created after the reports
choices.why: It was created first; the gap was after it.

choices.text: The fingerprint is random and changes each run
choices.why: It is md5 of the same rows; it does not change unless the rows do.

choices.text: The backup missed the last segment
choices.why: The copy matched the restore point exactly; the live side had moved on.

choices.text: The two sides were read at different moments
choices.why: Right. The live side was read after the moment the copy was restored to, and orders inserted in that instant were on one side only.

prompt: Why is a drill that sometimes fails for its own reasons dangerous?
hint: What do people learn from it?

choices.text: It uses up the restore server
choices.why: The cost is in trust, not machines.

choices.text: It deletes good backups
choices.why: A drill never touches the repository's backups.

choices.text: Its failures stop being read
choices.why: Right. People learn to ignore its failures, and then miss a real one. A red result has to always mean something.

choices.text: It slows the live server down
choices.why: That is a separate concern.

prompt: Which method makes the live report and the restored copy describe the same instant on a busy database?
hint: One snapshot, and its time.

choices.text: One snapshot, restored to its own now()
choices.why: Right: read the report in one REPEATABLE READ snapshot and restore to its now(). Every statement sees one instant, and the restore stops there.

choices.text: Run the report twice and keep the second result
choices.why: Two moving reads are still moving.

choices.text: Restore to the latest point the archive has
choices.why: The latest point keeps moving too.

choices.text: Lock every table during the drill
choices.why: That stops the application: an outage to run a check.

prompt: Between `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`, PostgreSQL's `now()` returns the moment the ___ started, which is why it can name a snapshot's time.
hint: Not the statement.

prompt: What does the interval between drills tell you?
hint: A backup breaks the day after a drill.

choices.text: How much data a restore loses
choices.why: That is the backup and archive's job, lesson 8's RPO.

choices.text: How long a broken backup goes unnoticed, at most
choices.why: Right. With monthly drills, up to a month.

choices.text: How long a restore takes
choices.why: The drill measures that; the interval does not decide it.

choices.text: How many backups are kept
choices.why: That is retention.

prompt: Retention keeps about two weeks of backups and the drill runs monthly. What happens when the drill finds that backups broke three weeks ago?
hint: Look at the figure.

choices.text: You restore from the last backup before the break
choices.why: It expired a week ago; retention reaches back two weeks.

choices.text: You restore from the newest backup, which is fine
choices.why: The newest backup is one of the broken ones.

choices.text: Every kept backup is from after the break, so none is good
choices.why: Right. The drill interval has to be shorter than the retention window.

choices.text: pgBackRest restores a backup from the expired set
choices.why: Expired backups are deleted from the repository.

prompt: Fulls are weekly, two are kept, and you want at least one week of margin between noticing a failure and the last good backup expiring. What is the longest drill interval in days?
hint: About fourteen days of retention, minus seven of margin.

prompt: What does a quarterly drill by a person who did not set the backups up catch that the weekly script cannot?
hint: The script never needs to ask anybody anything.

choices.text: Steps only one person knows
choices.why: Right: a procedure, a password or a step that lives in one person's head. A script that works says nothing about whether anybody else could do it.

choices.text: A backup damaged by a bad disk
choices.why: The weekly script's verify and restore catch that.

choices.text: A restore that is slower than last week
choices.why: drills.csv shows that trend.

choices.text: Changes in the fingerprint
choices.why: The script compares fingerprints every week.

prompt: Restore times in `drills.csv` rose from 20 minutes in January to 50 in June. The promise is one hour. What is the useful reading?
hint: Extend the line.

choices.text: Nothing to do while it is under an hour
choices.why: At that rate it passes the hour within months, and a restore on that day breaks the promise.

choices.text: The backups are degrading and must be retaken
choices.why: Slower is not damaged; the data grew.

choices.text: Drill less often, so the numbers stay stable
choices.why: The numbers would still grow; you would just stop seeing them.

choices.text: Act now: the trend will cross the promise soon
choices.why: Right. Faster restore hardware, parallel restore, or more frequent fulls, before the day it matters.

prompt: According to the lesson, what do real drills most often fail on?
hint: Usually before the data.

choices.text: A damaged backup file
choices.why: It happens, and it is the rarest of the list.

choices.text: Something the restore needs that is not with the backup
choices.why: Right: a key, a password, a configuration file, a tablespace, an extension.

choices.text: The fingerprint function giving different results on two machines
choices.why: md5 is deterministic everywhere.

choices.text: PostgreSQL refusing to replay archived log
choices.why: Replay works when the log is there; gaps are a separate, listed failure.

prompt: Match each drill finding with the kind of failure it is.
hint: Only one is the backup itself.

pairs.left: The restore server has PostgreSQL 15 installed
pairs.right: The restore machine is not ready

pairs.left: A segment from March is missing in the repository
Only Ana knows the repository's encryption password
pairs.right: Something the restore needs is not with the backup

pairs.left: A full backup fails its checksum

right_distractors: The live database is too slow
